parts.visual:
Three friends start a company. Person A had the idea. Person B is writing all the code. Person C put $5,000 into the bank account. How do they divide the 100% ownership (Equity) of the company?

The Equity Rules:
1. Ideas are worth nothing. Execution is everything.
2. Do not split 50/50 just to avoid an awkward conversation. Equity must be distributed based on future, long-term contribution to the company, not past favors.
parts.audio: Splitting equity is the first major test of a founding team. Dividing the company equally just to be 'nice' is a fatal mistake. Equity must reflect the brutal reality of who is going to build the most value over the next ten years.

questions.question: Person A says: 'I had the brilliant idea for this app, so I deserve 80% of the company. You guys just have to program it and sell it.' Why is this absurd?
options: Because an idea has zero economic value. The people executing the idea (building the code, selling the product) are taking all the risk and creating 99% of the value. The 'Idea Guy' is useless without execution.
questions.correct_answer: Because an idea has zero economic value. The people executing the idea (building the code, selling the product) are taking all the risk and creating 99% of the value. The 'Idea Guy' is useless without execution.
questions.explanation: Investors laugh at founders who demand a premium just for having an idea.

questions.question: Listen to the CEO arguing with their Co-Founder. What is the core disagreement over the 50/50 split?
questions.tts_text: We split it 50/50 because we are best friends. But I am working 80 hours a week, and you are keeping your safe corporate job and only working on this on Sundays. That is not a 50/50 partnership.
options: Asymmetric Risk and Effort. One founder has gone 'All-In', risking their entire livelihood, while the other is treating it like a hobby. A 50/50 split in this scenario will destroy the company through resentment.
The Co-Founder is a bad programmer.
questions.correct_answer: Asymmetric Risk and Effort. One founder has gone 'All-In', risking their entire livelihood, while the other is treating it like a hobby. A 50/50 split in this scenario will destroy the company through resentment.
questions.explanation: Equity must be proportional to risk.

questions.question: Why do VCs hate to see a company where the CEO only owns 10% of the equity, but a silent partner (who doesn't work there) owns 90%?
options: The Incentive Problem. If the CEO works for 10 years to build a billion-dollar company, but only gets 10% of the reward, they will eventually quit. VCs need the active founders to own the vast majority of the company.
Because the silent partner is rude.
questions.correct_answer: The Incentive Problem. If the CEO works for 10 years to build a billion-dollar company, but only gets 10% of the reward, they will eventually quit. VCs need the active founders to own the vast majority of the company.
questions.explanation: Dead equity (equity owned by people who don't contribute) kills startups.

questions.question: What is the danger of splitting a company exactly 50/50 between two founders?
options: Deadlock. If the two founders fundamentally disagree on a strategic decision (like selling the company), neither has the 51% majority to break the tie. The company becomes paralyzed and dies.
questions.correct_answer: Deadlock. If the two founders fundamentally disagree on a strategic decision (like selling the company), neither has the 51% majority to break the tie. The company becomes paralyzed and dies.
questions.explanation: Someone must have 51%. Someone has to be the boss.

questions.question: Order the words to describe the reality of startups:
questions.explanation: Never give 50% of your company to someone whose only contribution was 'the idea'.
